unit-alg-t4-02.title: Topic 4 · 4-2 Graphing Rational Functions
unit-alg-t4-02.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 4-2: Graphing Rational Functions

summary.text: Lesson 4-2 graphs rational functions: finding vertical asymptotes from the denominator, horizontal asymptotes by comparing degrees, rewriting (ax + b)/(cx + d) with long division to see the translation, graphs that cross a horizontal asymptote, and rational models such as a dosage rule.

why.text: Asymptotes are the skeleton of a rational graph: find them first and the curve almost draws itself. The same three-case degree comparison returns in calculus as the idea of a limit.

objectives.text: Find vertical asymptotes and holes by factoring the denominator
Find the horizontal asymptote by comparing the degrees of the numerator and denominator
Rewrite (ax + b)/(cx + d) as a translated reciprocal function and sketch it
Use a rational model to answer a question about a real situation

parentNote.text: The most common slip is treating every zero of the denominator as a vertical asymptote without factoring the numerator too — a shared factor makes a HOLE instead, and one question is built around exactly that error. The second is the myth that a graph can never cross an asymptote: that is only true of vertical ones, and the textbook spends a whole example on a graph crossing its horizontal asymptote.

nextUp.text: Learn the three degree cases for horizontal asymptotes first; they come up in almost every question.

cards.def:
**A function written as one polynomial divided by another, P(x)/Q(x), with Q(x) not the zero polynomial.**
• Its domain is every x where Q(x) ≠ 0.
• Rational numbers are ratios of integers; rational expressions are ratios of polynomials.
cards.hint: Polynomial over polynomial — nothing under a root, no variable exponents.

cards.def:
**x = a is a vertical asymptote when the denominator is 0 at a and the numerator is not.**
• Factor the denominator and set each factor equal to 0.
• Close to a, the values shoot off to +∞ or −∞; test a value on each side to see which.
cards.hint: Zero underneath, not zero on top.

cards.def:
**When a factor cancels from top and bottom, its zero is a hole in the graph, not a vertical asymptote.**
• (x − 2)(x + 4)/((x − 2)(x + 1)) has a hole at x = 2 and an asymptote only at x = −1.
• The x-value is still excluded from the domain — the graph just has a single missing point there.
cards.hint: Cancel first, then look for asymptotes.

cards.def:
**Compare degrees: top lower → y = 0; equal → y = ratio of the leading coefficients; top higher → no horizontal asymptote.**
• (3x + 1)/(x² + 4): bottom wins, so y = 0.
• (6x² − x)/(2x² + 5): a tie, so y = 6/2 = 3.
• (x³ + 1)/(4x − 1): top wins, so the values run off without settling.
cards.hint: Whichever degree is bigger wins the far-out race.

cards.term: Why the leading coefficients decide it
cards.def:
**Far from the origin only the highest-degree terms matter, so a tie in degree leaves the ratio of their coefficients.**
• For (8x + 3)/(4x − 1) with x = 1,000: 8,003/3,999 ≈ 2.001, closing in on 8/4 = 2.
• Substituting a huge x is a quick way to check any horizontal asymptote.
cards.hint: Plug in a very large x and watch where the values head.

cards.def:
**Long division turns (ax + b)/(x − h) into k + r/(x − h), which is 1/x stretched by r and moved to the asymptotes x = h and y = k.**
• (3x − 1)/(x − 2) = 3 + 5/(x − 2).
• It works exactly like turning an improper fraction into a mixed number.
cards.hint: The quotient is the horizontal asymptote; the remainder is the stretch.

cards.def:
**Draw the asymptotes x = −d/c and y = a/c first, then plot a couple of points on each side of the vertical one.**
• The asymptotes are your frame; the points tell you which corners the branches occupy.
• Add the intercepts: x-intercept where ax + b = 0, y-intercept at f(0) = b/d.
• Shown: (x + 1)/(x − 3), with asymptotes x = 3 and y = 1 and x-intercept (−1, 0).

**A denominator that factors into several pieces can give several vertical asymptotes — one for each zero that does not cancel.**
• (x + 2)/(x² − x − 12) = (x + 2)/((x − 4)(x + 3)): asymptotes at x = 4 and x = −3.
• The graph then has three pieces, not two.
cards.hint: Factor the bottom completely before you decide.

cards.term: A horizontal asymptote can be crossed
cards.def:
**Graphs may cross a horizontal asymptote in the middle; they can never cross a vertical one.**
• The horizontal asymptote only describes the far ends.
• To find a crossing, set f(x) equal to the asymptote value and solve.
• Shown: (x² + 2x)/(x² + 1) has asymptote y = 1 and crosses it at (½, 1).
cards.hint: Horizontal = end behaviour only. Vertical = a forbidden x.

cards.def:
**x-intercepts are where the numerator is 0 (and the denominator is not); the y-intercept is f(0).**
• A rational function may have no y-intercept at all, when x = 0 is excluded.
• A zero of the numerator that also zeroes the denominator is a hole, not an intercept.
cards.hint: Top = 0 for x-intercepts; x = 0 for the y-intercept.

cards.def:
**Average cost = (fixed cost + cost per item × x)/x, and its horizontal asymptote is the cost per item.**
• Spreading a big fixed cost over more items drives the average down toward the per-item cost, never below it.
• Its vertical asymptote x = 0 says: with nothing made, there is no average.
cards.hint: The fixed cost thins out; the per-item cost never does.

cards.def:
**To solve f(x) ≥ c for a rational model, graph y = f(x) and y = c and read where the curve is on or above the line.**
• Or clear the denominator algebraically — but only after checking its sign.
• In a real model, keep only the inputs that make sense (ages, amounts and times are not negative).
cards.hint: Intersection first, then the side of it you want.

questions.q: Which of these is a rational function?
questions.hint: Both top and bottom must be polynomials.
steps: A rational function is a polynomial divided by a polynomial.
√x is not a polynomial, |x| is not a polynomial, and 2ˣ has the variable in the exponent.
x + 5 and x² − 9 are both polynomials.
f(x) = (x + 5)/(x² − 9) is the rational function.

ex.main: **f(x) = (x + 5)/(x² − 9).** Polynomial over polynomial. Each of the others breaks the rule in a different place: a radical on top, an absolute value underneath, and an exponential on top.
ex.tip: A rational function can still have a messy domain — that is what its asymptotes are about.

questions.q: What is the vertical asymptote of f(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 7)?
questions.hint: Set the denominator equal to zero.
steps: The denominator is x − 7.
x − 7 = 0 when x = 7.
The numerator is 8 there, not 0, so it is an asymptote rather than a hole.
The vertical asymptote is x = 7.

ex.main: **x = 7.** The bottom is zero there and the top is not. x = −1 is where the TOP is zero — that is the x-intercept — and y = 1 is the horizontal asymptote.
ex.tip: Denominator zero → vertical asymptote; numerator zero → x-intercept.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (6x − 1)/(3x + 2)?
questions.hint: Compare the degrees of the top and the bottom.
steps: Both top and bottom have degree 1 — a tie.
A tie means the asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients.
That ratio is 6/3.
The horizontal asymptote is y = 2.

ex.main: **y = 2.** Equal degrees, so divide the leading coefficients: 6 ÷ 3. y = −1/2 divides the constant terms, which matter near the origin but vanish far out; y = 0 is the rule for when the bottom has the HIGHER degree.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (x + 4)/(x² + 1)?
questions.hint: Which has the higher degree, top or bottom?
steps: The top has degree 1; the bottom has degree 2.
The bottom grows much faster, so the fraction shrinks toward 0.
When the bottom has the higher degree, the asymptote is y = 0.
The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

ex.main: **y = 0.** The bottom's x² outruns the top's x, so far out the fraction shrinks toward zero. y = 1 would need equal degrees, and "there is none" is the case when the TOP has the higher degree.
ex.tip: Bottom-heavy fractions always settle on y = 0.

questions.q: What is the horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (x³ − 2)/(5x + 1)?
questions.hint: Compare degrees: 3 against 1.
steps: The top has degree 3; the bottom has degree 1.
The top outgrows the bottom, so the values keep growing without settling.
A top-heavy rational function has no horizontal asymptote.
None.

ex.main: **None.** With the higher degree on top, f(x) runs off to ±∞ instead of levelling out. y = 1/5 would need a tie in degree, and y = 0 would need the bottom to win.
ex.tip: Top-heavy → no horizontal asymptote.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = 2x/(x² − 5x + 6)?
questions.hint: Factor the denominator and find its zeros.
steps: It is zero at x = 2 and at x = 3.
Those two inputs are excluded.
The domain is all real numbers except 2 and 3.

ex.main: **All real numbers except 2 and 3.** Those are the zeros of (x − 2)(x − 3). −2 and −3 come from reading the signs in the factors instead of solving, and 0 is where the NUMERATOR is zero, which is perfectly allowed.
ex.tip: Zeros of the numerator are allowed; zeros of the denominator are not.

questions.q: Which statement about the asymptotes of a rational function is true?
opts: Its graph can cross a vertical asymptote but never a horizontal one
Its graph can never cross either kind of asymptote at any point
Its graph can cross a horizontal asymptote but never a vertical one
Its graph can cross both kinds of asymptote as often as it likes
questions.hint: What does each kind of asymptote actually describe?
steps: A vertical asymptote x = a marks an input the function cannot take.
So the graph has no point at all on that line.
A horizontal asymptote only describes where the values settle far left and far right.
In the middle of the graph, the curve is free to cross it.

ex.main: **It can cross a horizontal asymptote but never a vertical one.** A vertical asymptote is an excluded x-value, so no point of the graph can sit on it. A horizontal asymptote is a statement about the far ends only, and plenty of graphs cross it in the middle before settling.
ex.tip: "Never crosses an asymptote" is a myth that only holds for the vertical kind.

questions.q: Rewrite f(x) = (5x + 2)/(x − 1) in the form k + r/(x − h).
questions.hint: Divide x − 1 into 5x + 2 and keep the remainder.
steps: 5x ÷ x = 5, so the quotient is 5.
(5x + 2) − (5x − 5) = 7, the remainder.

ex.main: **5 + 7/(x − 1).** So the graph is 1/x stretched by 7 and moved to the asymptotes x = 1 and y = 5. "5 + 2/(x − 1)" forgets to subtract 5(x − 1); "5 − 7/(x − 1)" subtracts the wrong way round.
ex.tip: Check by recombining: 5(x − 1) + 7 = 5x + 2.

questions.q: What are the vertical asymptotes of f(x) = (x + 2)/(x² + x − 12)?
questions.hint: Factor x² + x − 12.
steps: The zeros are x = −4 and x = 3.
The numerator x + 2 is not zero at either, so neither is a hole.
The vertical asymptotes are x = −4 and x = 3.

ex.main: **x = −4 and x = 3.** (x + 4)(x − 3) is zero at both. x = 4 and x = −3 copy the signs out of the factors without solving, and x = −2 is the numerator's zero — the x-intercept.
ex.tip: Solve each factor = 0; never read the answer straight off the sign.

questions.q: What does the graph of f(x) = (x − 5)/(x² − 2x − 15) have at x = 5 and at x = −3?
opts: A vertical asymptote at both x = 5 and x = −3
A hole at x = 5 and a vertical asymptote at x = −3
A vertical asymptote at x = 5 and a hole at x = −3
A hole at both x = 5 and x = −3, and no asymptote
questions.hint: Factor the bottom and look for a factor that cancels.
steps: f(x) = (x − 5)/((x − 5)(x + 3)), and the x − 5 cancels.
A cancelled factor leaves a hole; what remains, 1/(x + 3), has an asymptote at x = −3.
Hole at x = 5, vertical asymptote at x = −3.

ex.main: **A hole at x = 5 and a vertical asymptote at x = −3.** Both values are excluded from the domain, but they look different on the graph: the cancelled factor leaves a single missing point, while the factor that survives makes the values shoot off to infinity.
ex.tip: Cancel first, then decide which zeros are holes and which are asymptotes.

questions.q: What are the intercepts of f(x) = (2x − 6)/(x + 3)?
questions.hint: Numerator zero for the x-intercept; x = 0 for the y-intercept.
steps: 2x − 6 = 0 gives x = 3, and the denominator is 6 there, not 0.
So the x-intercept is (3, 0).
The y-intercept is (0, −2).

ex.main: **(3, 0) and (0, −2).** (−3, 0) uses the denominator's zero, which is the vertical asymptote — the function does not even exist there. (0, 2) drops the sign of −6, and x = 0 is a perfectly allowed input here, so there is a y-intercept.
ex.tip: An x-intercept can never come from the denominator.

questions.q: The graph shown has its asymptotes drawn in and crosses the x-axis at x = −½. Which function does it show?
questions.hint: Read the vertical asymptote, then the horizontal one, then check each option against both.
steps: The vertical asymptote is x = 2, so the denominator is zero at 2: x − 2.
The horizontal asymptote is y = 2, so the leading coefficients must divide to 2.
(2x + 1)/(x − 2) has both, and its numerator is zero at x = −½.
The graph shows f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 2).

ex.main: **f(x) = (2x + 1)/(x − 2).** (2x + 1)/(x + 2) has the right horizontal asymptote but its vertical one is at x = −2. (x + 1)/(x − 2) has the right vertical asymptote but settles at y = 1. (x − 2)/(2x + 1) is the reciprocal: asymptotes x = −½ and y = ½.
ex.tip: Two asymptotes usually narrow it to one option; the intercept confirms it.

questions.q: f(x) = (2x² + x)/(x² − 9) has horizontal asymptote y = 2. Where, if anywhere, does its graph cross that asymptote?
questions.hint: Set f(x) equal to 2 and solve.
steps: Multiply by x² − 9: 2x² + x = 2x² − 18.
The 2x² terms cancel, leaving x = −18.
x = −18 is not ±3, so it is allowed: the graph crosses y = 2 at x = −18.

ex.main: **At x = −18.** Far out to the left the graph comes in from just above or below y = 2 and passes through it at (−18, 2) before settling. "It never crosses" is the myth from the vertical kind of asymptote; x = 0 is where the graph crosses the x-axis, not y = 2.
ex.tip: Crossing a horizontal asymptote is just an ordinary equation: set f(x) = k.

questions.q: An app costs $60,000 to build and $0.50 per download to deliver, so its average cost per download is C(x) = (60,000 + 0.5x)/x. What does the horizontal asymptote of C say?
opts: y = 60,000: the average cost levels off at $60,000 per download
y = 0.5: the average cost falls toward $0.50 and never reaches it
y = 0: with enough downloads, each one costs almost nothing
None exists: the average cost keeps falling forever with no limit
questions.hint: Both top and bottom have degree 1. Compare their leading coefficients.
steps: The top is 0.5x + 60,000 and the bottom is x: equal degrees.
The ratio of leading coefficients is 0.5 ÷ 1 = 0.5.
Far out, the $60,000 is spread so thin it hardly matters, but every download still costs $0.50.
The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.5.

ex.main: **y = 0.5.** C(x) = 0.5 + 60,000/x, and the second term shrinks toward 0 as downloads pile up, leaving the $0.50 that every single download costs. It never reaches $0.50, because some of the build cost is always in the average.
ex.tip: In an average-cost model, the asymptote is the cost nobody can spread away.

questions.q: Which function has vertical asymptotes x = −1 and x = 4, and horizontal asymptote y = 2?
questions.hint: Build the denominator from the vertical asymptotes, then match the degrees for y = 2.
steps: x = −1 and x = 4 need the factors (x + 1) and (x − 4) underneath.
That denominator has degree 2 and leading coefficient 1.
For y = 2, the top must also have degree 2 with leading coefficient 2: 2x².
f(x) = 2x²/((x + 1)(x − 4)), and 2x² is not zero at −1 or 4.

ex.main: **f(x) = 2x²/((x + 1)(x − 4)).** 2x/(…) has a lower-degree top, so its asymptote is y = 0. The (x − 1)(x + 4) versions put the vertical asymptotes at x = 1 and x = −4 — the sign trap again.
ex.tip: Many functions fit these asymptotes. Any top of the form 2x² + bx + c works, as long as it is not zero at −1 or 4.

questions.q: A child's dose of a medicine is D(a) = 300a/(a + 12) milligrams, where a is the age in years, and the dose grows with age. At what age is the dose exactly 120 mg?
questions.hint: Set 300a/(a + 12) equal to 120 and clear the denominator.
steps: Multiply both sides by a + 12: 300a = 120a + 1,440.
a = 8 years.

ex.main: **8 years.** Check: D(8) = 2,400/20 = 120 mg. 4.8 years is 120 × 12 ÷ 300, which loses the a in the denominator; 0.4 years ignores the denominator entirely (300a = 120); 12 years mistakes the 12 in the formula for the answer.
ex.tip: Clear the denominator by multiplying EVERY term on both sides by it.

questions.q: For f(x) = 1/(x − 3)², what happens as x approaches 3 from each side?
opts: f(x) → +∞ from both the left and the right
f(x) → −∞ from the left and +∞ from the right
f(x) → +∞ from the left and −∞ from the right
f(x) → 0 from both the left and the right
questions.hint: What sign does a square have?
steps: Near x = 3, (x − 3)² is a tiny number.
A square is never negative, so it is a tiny POSITIVE number on both sides.
1 divided by a tiny positive number is a huge positive number.
f(x) → +∞ from both sides.

ex.main: **+∞ from both sides.** The square makes the denominator positive whichever side you come from, so both pieces of the graph shoot upward. Opposite directions on the two sides is the behaviour of 1/(x − 3), whose denominator changes sign at 3.
ex.tip: Test one value each side — 2.9 and 3.1 — whenever you are unsure.

questions.q: Which function has the horizontal asymptote y = −3?
questions.hint: You need equal degrees AND leading coefficients that divide to −3.
steps: (−3x + 1)/(x + 5): equal degrees, −3 ÷ 1 = −3.
(3x + 1)/(x − 5): equal degrees, but 3 ÷ 1 = 3.
(x − 3)/(x + 5): equal degrees, 1 ÷ 1 = 1 — the −3 is a constant, which does not count.
(−3x² + 1)/(x + 5): the top has the higher degree, so there is no horizontal asymptote.

ex.main: **f(x) = (−3x + 1)/(x + 5).** Every option contains a 3; only one puts −3 on the LEADING terms with the degrees tied. The squared version is the subtle one: the leading coefficient is right, but the degrees are not equal.
ex.tip: Degrees first, coefficients second.

questions.q: A classmate says f(x) = (x² + 2x − 8)/(x² − 4) has vertical asymptotes x = 2 and x = −2 and horizontal asymptote y = 1. What is wrong?
opts: There is no horizontal asymptote, because the two degrees are equal
The horizontal asymptote should be y = 2, from the 2x in the numerator
x = 2 is a hole, not an asymptote; only x = −2 is a vertical asymptote
Nothing is wrong — both vertical asymptotes and y = 1 are correct
questions.hint: Factor top and bottom before deciding anything.
steps: The factor x − 2 cancels, leaving (x + 4)/(x + 2) with a hole at x = 2.
Only x + 2 survives underneath, so x = −2 is the one vertical asymptote.
The degrees tie with leading coefficients 1 and 1, so y = 1 is right.

ex.main: **x = 2 is a hole, not an asymptote.** The classmate found the zeros of the denominator without checking the numerator. y = 1 is correct, and equal degrees give the ratio of leading coefficients, not "no asymptote".
ex.tip: Always factor the top too — a shared factor turns an asymptote into a hole.

questions.q: A jug holds 10 litres of juice that is 40% fruit, so 4 litres are fruit. After x litres of water are added, the fruit fraction is F(x) = 4/(10 + x). How much water makes the drink 25% fruit?
questions.hint: Set 4/(10 + x) equal to 0.25.
steps: Add 6 litres of water.

ex.main: **6 litres.** Check: 4 out of 16 litres is 25%. 16 litres is the TOTAL volume, not the water added; 15 comes from 40 − 25; 2.5 litres is 25% of the original 10.
ex.tip: Once you have an answer, plug it back into the model — it takes five seconds.
